problem: Object-goal navigation work mostly targets static objects and either uses end-to-end map-free policies with high sample complexity and a sim-to-real gap, or purely geometric coverage planners that ignore where a given movable object is likely to be.
motivation: Household objects such as keys, glasses and phones change position with human activity, so a robot should search likely places first, as people do. A modular, map-based design with a learned per-object likelihood map is sample-efficient and lets detectors and planners be swapped between sim and real.
key_idea: A contextual bandit with optimism under uncertainty learns online the probability of spotting each object from each sampled vantage point, and these probabilities act as weights in a Weighted Minimum Latency Problem solver that orders the vantage points to visit.
insight: Ground-truth likelihood scores beat the geometry-only TSP planner in all environments, so modeling where the target object is likely to be matters beyond room geometry. The one-step greedy planner often matches or beats CP-SAT under a 30 s budget, especially in the larger, cluttered Kitchen 2 (SPL 0.26 Gen-Lin greedy vs 0.29 CP-SAT, 0.25 vs 0.20 Neural). The per-class Gen-Lin model often outperforms the shared-parameter Neural model, since it has an easier learning problem.
method: Vantage point sampling: extract navigable points from the 2D occupancy map (0.1 m resolution) and pick k (25 or 50) with Farthest Point Sub-sampling under Euclidean distance.

Contextual bandit importance estimation: each vantage point is an arm with features (one-hot target object, a flattened 16x16 wall-distance-map patch, sinusoidal positional encoding); the estimate uses a lower confidence bound sigma(theta^T phi - eps) from a generalized linear model (online Newton step, per-class parameters) or a two-layer NTK-approximated neural net (shared across classes).
Positive sample augmentation: once the object is spotted and triangulated, all navigable points within r_vis of it receive a +1 signal to speed up learning.

WMLP planning: order the vantage points to minimize expected weighted latency, either with the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver (30 s budget) or a one-step greedy rule maximizing alpha_p/dist + (1-alpha_p)*p_hat.
Execution: MPC drives the robot along the planned path while a ViLD detector inspects the surroundings (r_vis 2.5 m at eval), and the robot heads to the object once it is spotted.
Theory: a regret bound of O(k^2 D sqrt(T)) for a variant with a projection step and epsilon-cover under a generalized linear model.
Hyperparameter tuning: Vizier GP-bandit optimization of SPL over training episodes.

setting.backbone: Contextual bandit (generalized linear model or two-layer NTK neural net), CP-SAT / greedy WMLP planner, ViLD detector, MPC controller
setting.training_data: Online learning for 200 episodes in the same simulated kitchen; the real-kitchen model is trained on a simulated snapshot of the map; no external data
setting.observation: 2D occupancy map plus onboard depth/LiDAR and RGB with an open-vocabulary detector (ViLD)
setting.action_space: Waypoints (vantage points) visited via A* distances and MPC low-level control
setting.simulator: Bullet physics simulator with Matterport-scan scenes (two simulated kitchens); real office kitchen
setting.privileged: Known 2D occupancy map; ground-truth object likelihoods only in the GT-Scores upper-bound variants; target object identity given

numbers.eval_set_note: 300 evaluation episodes, 5 object classes, 25 vantage points

numbers_note: Custom benchmarks (own kitchens), so no canonical benchmark. Other variants (Neural in sim, GT-Scores, TSP baseline, peaky distribution in the appendix) are in the tables but not all listed. Values are fractions as printed (0-1).
results: Learned-likelihood agents beat the geometric TSP baseline in SPL, e.g. Kitchen 1 Gen-Lin CP-SAT 0.47 vs TSP 0.38, and Kitchen 2 0.29 vs 0.22. They approach the GT-Scores upper bounds (0.51 and 0.34). In the real kitchen, Neural + CP-SAT reaches 0.92 success and 0.42 SPL vs TSP 0.88 / 0.37.
limitations: Sensitive to detection failures, WMLP solver slowness, and early stopping of CP-SAT, which yields poor solutions.
The NTK approximation limits the network architecture of the Neural model.
Evaluation is small-scale (two simulated kitchens, one real kitchen, 5 object classes, task-specific SPL), and success rates and SPL are modest.
